sql:
SELECT z.LocationID, z.Borough, z.Zone, COUNT(t.PULocationID) AS cash_trips
FROM ops.zones z
LEFT JOIN lake.trips t ON t.PULocationID = z.LocationID AND t.payment_type = 2
GROUP BY z.LocationID, z.Borough, z.Zone
ORDER BY z.LocationID

FROM ops.zones z

    FROM lake.trips

    GROUP BY PULocationID
) agg ON agg.PULocationID = z.LocationID
ORDER BY z.LocationID

diagnosis.bottleneck: The query spends most of its time scanning the entire trips table (495,833 rows) to apply the payment_type=2 filter, which reduces the row count to ~99,167 before the join and aggregation.

plan_nodes.note: Join Type: RIGHT | Conditions: CAST(PULocationID AS BIGINT) = LocationID | Estimated Cardinality: 99167

hypotheses.claim: A filter on the joined side sits in the ON clause of a LEFT JOIN; the join dominates the cost. (matched: left join lake.trips t on … and t.payment_type = 2)

The sequential scan on trips reads all rows and filters on payment_type=2; because payment_type has only 5 distinct values, a columnar zone map or partitioning on payment_type could avoid scanning irrelevant row groups.
The hash join condition includes a CAST(PULocationID AS BIGINT) = LocationID, which adds per-row CPU overhead; aligning the data types of the join keys would eliminate the cast.
The hash group by processes 99,167 rows; while this is small, if the hash table exceeds memory and spills to disk, it could become a bottleneck.
